title: Weekly Review and Systems
summary: Capture every task in one trusted place, run a weekly review, understand why you procrastinate, and manage deadlines with buffers.
objectives: Set up a single capture system and a 30-minute weekly review.
Name your procrastination type and apply a matching fix.
Set personal deadlines ahead of real ones using buffers.

explanation.heading: A system you trust
explanation.body:
So far you have audited your time, blocked your days and protected your focus. All of that decays without a system that keeps everything in one place and returns to it every week. Without it, commitments sit in your head, which is a poor storage device: they nag you at night but are forgotten in the morning.

**Capture** means that every task, idea or promise goes into one trusted inbox the moment it appears: a notes app, a small notebook, or a task list. The rule is one inbox, not five. Later, you sort the inbox into next actions, calendar items and things to drop. Example: during a lecture you remember to email the HOD about the project guide. Write "email HOD re guide" in the inbox in ten seconds and carry on listening.

explanation.heading: The weekly review
explanation.body:
The **weekly review** is a 30-minute appointment, say Sunday at 6 pm, that keeps the system alive. Follow the same steps each time:

1. Empty the inbox: turn each item into a next action, a calendar entry, or delete it.
2. Look back: what got done, what slipped, and why.
3. Look ahead: check next week's calendar for deadlines, exams and travel.
4. Choose the next week's top three outcomes and block time for them.
5. Clear clutter: close old tabs, tidy files, delete dead tasks.

Students often skip the review when busy, which is exactly when it matters most. If you only have ten minutes, do steps 1 and 4.

explanation.heading: Why we procrastinate
explanation.body:
Procrastination is usually avoidance of a feeling, not laziness. Common types and fixes:

- **Perfectionist**: afraid the result will be poor, so you never start. Fix: set a rough-draft rule and a 20-minute limit for version one.
- **Overwhelmed**: the task is too big. Fix: shrink it to the next physical action such as "open the file and write the title".
- **Bored**: the task is dull. Fix: pair it with a reward or a timer, or do it in a group study session.
- **Dreader**: the task triggers anxiety, such as emailing a senior. Fix: draft the message, then send it before you can reconsider.
- **Last-minute rusher**: needs pressure to move. Fix: create earlier fake deadlines with an accountability partner.

Naming your type tells you which fix to try instead of just scolding yourself.

explanation.heading: Deadlines and buffers
explanation.body:
Real deadlines are the finish line, not the target. Set a **personal deadline** earlier than the real one: for a submission due on the 30th, aim for the 25th. The gap is your **buffer** for illness, a failed laptop, a power cut or reviewer feedback. Work backwards: draft by the 15th, review by the 20th, final by the 25th.

If you cannot make a deadline, tell the person early and propose a new date with a reason. Silence until the last hour hurts trust; an early heads-up is a sign of reliability. Example: on the 22nd you realise your report needs three more days. You email your guide that day: "I may need until the 28th for the final report; the draft will reach you on the 25th."

examples.title: A Sunday review in 30 minutes
examples.body: Isha opens her inbox with 14 items. She converts 8 into next actions, puts 3 on the calendar and deletes 3. She notes that last week's SQL practice slipped due to a cousin's wedding, so she moves it to Tuesday evening. She picks three outcomes for next week, blocks them, and closes the session by checking Monday's classes.
examples.takeaway: The review turns a messy inbox into a calendar and a short list of priorities.

examples.title: Matching the fix to the type
examples.body: Rohit keeps avoiding an email to his internship coordinator. He notices it is dread, not lack of time. He types a three-line draft, sets a 10-minute timer, and sends it at the end of the timer. The reply arrives the next morning and was polite and short.
examples.takeaway: Once you name the real reason, the fix is small and concrete, not a lecture to yourself.

exercises.prompt: What is the main purpose of a single capture system?
options: To get commitments out of your head into one trusted place
To remember everything perfectly in your head
To make your to-do list longer
exercises.why: Capture frees your mind of nagging commitments. A single inbox is easier to trust than several, and it does not replace planning.

exercises.prompt: The first step of a weekly review is to ____ your inbox. (one word)
exercises.why: You start by emptying or processing the inbox into actions, calendar items or deletions.

exercises.prompt: You keep postponing your project report because you worry it will not be good enough. Which fix suits you best?

options.feedback: Waiting for a mood rarely arrives and the perfectionism stays.

options.text: Write a deliberately rough first version in 20 minutes and improve it later.
options.feedback: A rough-draft rule removes the fear of judgement and gets you moving.
This is not laziness and shame usually deepens avoidance.

options.text: Ask a friend to write it instead.
options.feedback: This avoids the task entirely and may cause integrity problems.

exercises.why: Perfectionist avoidance responds to a time-limited rough draft, not to willpower or waiting.

exercises.prompt: You have a project submission due on 30 November and today is 1 November. Write a backward plan with at least three dated checkpoints, a personal deadline earlier than the real one, and one sentence you would send to your guide if you were running late on 22 November.

descriptors.3: Three or more dates in logical backward order.
Clearly earlier with a reason for the buffer.
Early, specific new date and what you will deliver before it.

exercises.modelAnswer: Plan: topic and outline by 8 Nov, working prototype by 16 Nov, report draft by 22 Nov, review and fixes by 26 Nov. Personal deadline 26 Nov, giving four days of buffer for illness or feedback. Message: "I may need until 28 November for the final report, but you will have the working draft by 24 November."
exercises.guidance: A strong answer works backward from a deadline that is earlier than the real one and sends bad news early with a concrete new date. Mistakes include equal gaps that ignore review time and messages that only apologise. Compare against the model answer honestly.

Do the five-step weekly review in 30 minutes.
Choose three outcomes for next week and block time for them.

quiz.prompt: Where should a new task go the moment it appears?
quiz.why: One trusted inbox prevents lost tasks.

quiz.prompt: How long should a regular weekly review take roughly?
quiz.why: About half an hour is enough and easy to keep.

quiz.prompt: Which fix suits someone overwhelmed by a huge task?
options: Shrink it to the next physical action
quiz.why: A tiny first step removes the paralysis.

quiz.prompt: Why set a personal deadline before the real one?
options: Because the real one is unfair
quiz.why: The gap absorbs illness, tech failures and feedback.

bank.prompt: You remember mid-conversation that you must book a train ticket. What is the best immediate action?
options: Jot it in your inbox within seconds
bank.why: Quick capture lets you stay present and still keep the commitment.

bank.prompt: Avoiding a task because it triggers anxiety, such as emailing a senior, is the ____ type of procrastination. (one word)
bank.why: Dread-driven avoidance responds to drafting and sending the message in a short, timed burst.

bank.prompt: The real deadline is 20 March. You aim to finish by 15 March. What is the 5-day gap called?
bank.why: A buffer is slack you create before the true deadline.

cards.back: One trusted inbox where every task and promise goes immediately, then sorted later.
Empty the inbox, look back, look ahead, choose next week outcomes, clear clutter, in about 30 minutes.
Perfectionist, overwhelmed, bored, dreader and last-minute rusher, each with a matching small fix.
Set personal deadlines earlier than real ones, work backward with checkpoints, and warn people early with a new date if you will be late.

reflection: Which procrastination type is yours most often, and what single small fix will you apply this week?

keyPoints: Use one inbox and capture instantly.
Review weekly in 30 minutes and plan the next week.
Match your procrastination type with a small fix.
Set earlier personal deadlines and warn early when late.
